## 1. Breakdown of the 6 Side Symbols

Flanking George Eastman’s central portrait profile are **six small square bronze panels** (three on the left, three on the right). Designed in an Art Deco, low-relief style, each symbol represents a foundational pillar of Eastman’s life, industry, and philosophy.

```
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Top-Left:           |   | Top-Right:          |
| Light Rays & Prism  |   | Woven Film Web      |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Middle-Left:        |   | Middle-Right:       |
| Chemical Retort     |   | Torches of Learning |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+
| Bottom-Left:        |   | Bottom-Right:       |
| Mechanical Gears    |   | Globe & Meridian    |
+---------------------+   +---------------------+

```

### Top-Left: Light Rays through a Prism (Optics & Physics)

* **Visual:** Stylized linear rays of light passing through a refraction angle / lens geometry.
* **Meaning:** Represents the physics of light and optics, the fundamental scientific basis of photography. It reflects Eastman’s obsession with capturing light accurately through precision lenses and exposure control.

* **Visual:** A classic glass chemical retort/flask resting over heat or set against laboratory lines.
* **Meaning:** Represents chemistry and emulsion technology. Eastman’s greatest breakthrough was transforming heavy, messy wet-plate photography into dry gelatin plates and flexible roll film through continuous chemical experimentation.

before.text: Twenty-five years later, on the evening of March 5, 1912, he sat down at the Hotel Belmont in New York with the president of MIT. The institute was financially strapped and Harvard was maneuvering to absorb it, and the two men talked into the night about a new campus across the Charles. Eastman asked what sum would be needed. Two and a half million, Maclaurin said. Eastman said he would send a draft for that amount. His only condition was that nobody know who had sent it. May I tell my wife, Maclaurin asked. Well, yes, Eastman said, but no one else. The secret held for eight years, and he asked for nothing in return: no name on any building, no publicity, no say in anything.

notes.text: what did he see in MIT?
notes.chunk_at_written: He gave away the bulk of a fortune while he was alive rather than leaving a foundation behind him, and much of it anonymously. In 1912, with MIT financially strapped and Harvard maneuvering to absorb it, he gave the institute two and a half million dollars under the name Mr. Smith. The money built the new Cambridge campus and left MIT solvent enough to refuse Harvard's terms. He kept the secret for eight years. That same year he bought a company in London in order to acquire one scientist, and told him his job was the future of photography. That laboratory produced Kodachrome, and color is what turned a photograph from a record into a memory.
